A2.text:
Nigar is a music student. Last month, she moved into an old building in the centre of Baku. Her flat is small, but she loves the green courtyard. She is a tenant, and the landlord, Mr Vugar, lives on the first floor.

Every evening, Nigar plays the violin for two hours. One morning, she found a note under her door. It said: “Please stop the noise at night!” It was a noise complaint.

Nigar was sad. She thought about her neighbour, Mr Agil. He is old and very quiet. His rule is “keep yourself to yourself”, and he never says hello. “It is him,” she thought.

A week later, Nigar saw Mr Agil on the stairs. He had two heavy bags of shopping. She wanted to lend a hand, so she carried the bags to his door.

Inside his flat, Nigar saw an old piano and many photos of children with violins.

“I was a music teacher for forty years,” Mr Agil said. “I did not write that note. I open my window every evening to listen to you.”

“Then who wrote it?” Nigar asked.

Mr Agil smiled. “In this building, the walls have ears. It was Sona on the second floor. Her baby sleeps at nine.”

Now Nigar plays from seven to nine. On Sundays, she plays in the courtyard. Mr Agil helps to look after the chairs, and Sona's baby dances.

B1.text:
When Nigar, a second-year violin student, rented a flat in an old building near Fountain Square, she fell in love with the courtyard first: a fig tree, washing lines and a tap where neighbours stopped to chat. The landlord, Mr Vugar, lived downstairs and promised her it was a friendly neighbourhood. “Everybody here gets along,” he said.

For three weeks she practised every evening. Then one morning a folded note appeared under her door: “Some of us need to sleep. Please stop the noise at night!” It wasn't signed, but it was clearly a noise complaint.

Nigar's first suspect was Mr Agil from across the landing. He was an elderly man who kept himself to himself. He nodded on the stairs but never started a conversation, and his curtains were always half closed. “Of course it's him,” she told her friend on the phone.

A few days later she found him stopping every few steps with two heavy shopping bags. However annoyed she felt, she couldn't walk past. “Let me lend a hand,” she said, and took the bags.

His flat surprised her. There was an upright piano, shelves of sheet music and framed photos of children holding tiny violins. “Forty years at the music school,” he explained. “And no, I didn't write that note. I open my window every evening to hear you play. You rush the slow parts, by the way.”

Nigar laughed, embarrassed. “Then who did?”

“In this building, the walls have ears,” he said. “Sona on the second floor has a new baby. She asked Vugar to write it because she was too shy.”

Nigar knocked on Sona's door that afternoon. They agreed on a simple deal: music until nine, silence after. Now, on Sunday evenings, Nigar plays in the courtyard. Mr Agil looks after the chairs, Sona brings tea, and the baby claps — mostly in time.

B2.text:
Nigar signed the lease for the flat near Fountain Square on the strength of the courtyard alone: a crooked fig tree, washing lines strung between balconies and a stone tap where neighbours lingered to swap news. Mr Vugar, the landlord, who lived on the ground floor, assured her that the community was close-knit. “Tenants come and go,” he said, “but in this building, we all get along.”

For three weeks, the second-year violin student practised every evening, working through the same difficult sonata until her fingers ached. Then, one morning, a folded sheet of paper appeared under her door: “Some of us have to sleep. Please stop the noise at night!” There was no signature, but there was no mistaking a noise complaint.

Her suspicion fell immediately on Mr Agil, the elderly widower across the landing. He kept himself to himself to an almost theatrical degree: a polite nod on the stairs, curtains permanently half drawn, never a word more than necessary. “It's obviously him,” she told a friend. “He looks at me as if I'm a mosquito.”

Yet when she later found him pausing on every third step, weighed down by two bulging shopping bags, irritation lost to upbringing. “Let me lend a hand,” she offered, and took them before he could refuse.

His flat stopped her in the doorway. An upright piano, its lid open; shelves sagging with sheet music; dozens of photographs of children clutching tiny violins. “Forty years at the music school,” he said, following her gaze. “And no, I didn't write your note. I open my window every evening to listen. You rush the slow movement, incidentally.”

She laughed despite herself. “Then who on earth did?”

He lowered his voice. “In this building, the walls have ears. Sona, on the second floor, has a newborn. She was too shy to knock, so she asked Vugar to write it for her.”

That afternoon Nigar climbed the stairs with a box of pakhlava. The negotiation took four minutes: music until nine, silence afterwards. These days, on Sunday evenings, she performs in the courtyard. Mr Agil looks after the chairs and offers unrequested advice on tempo, Sona brings a pot of tea, and the baby claps along — enthusiastically, if not always in rhythm.
